QF.id: XIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_28

question.text: In the context of IR futures, what does '100 minus yield' pricing convention mean?

answer.text: Short-term interest rate futures (like T-Bill futures) are quoted as 100 minus the annualized yield, so a yield of 6% gives a price of 94.00 — this means prices rise when yields fall
The futures price is always Rs 100 minus the spot bond price
The maximum loss on an IR futures position is limited to 100 minus the entry price
The futures contract expires worthless if yield exceeds 100%

explanation.text: The Logic: For 91-day T-Bill futures the quotation convention is 100 minus the futures discount yield. If yield is 5.5%, price is 94.50; if yield falls to 5.0%, price rises to 95.00. A long position therefore profits when yields fall, mirroring the inverse price-rate relationship. The Trap: The 100-minus-yield convention applies to short-term rate futures like 91-day T-Bills, not to bond futures, which are quoted directly in price terms. Note: Tick values differ by contract — the 91-day T-Bill futures tick value is Rs 1.25 per lot; the Rs 5 per basis-point figure relates to GOI bond futures and should not be applied to T-Bill futures.
